name: Japan
summary: Larry finished his service in Japan as a medical-evacuation patient. By his account (August 2026 call), he was flown out of Vietnam seriously ill — likely hepatitis, plus malaria and infections — arriving, as he remembers it, in early September 1965, with the weather turning cold into winter. His DD-214 independently confirms the Japan chapter: his last duty assignment was a U.S. Army medical command at APO SF 96343 (Camp Zama) under U.S. Army Japan. From the hospital he befriended the patient in the bed across from him, a man from back east whose name he no longer remembers; together they explored Tokyo, finding a basement German restaurant called "Heidelberg" off the Ginza. Japan is also where he remembers seeing the Stars and Stripes item reporting him killed in action. In a Tell a Story comment (2026-08-13) he named the hospital himself: "I was at Camp Zama in Japan in Sugami Uro" [read as Sagami-Ōno].
larrysRecollection: Around August 1965, Larry was in Japan. He personally remembers seeing a notice or article in Stars and Stripes saying he had been killed. He went to Japan because he was sick — "sepititis" [as noted; likely hepatitis], malaria, and infections — and lost a bunch of weight; his stool was pure white and his urine looked like Coca-Cola. The weather was cold, going into winter; he placed it as early September. The man in his Japan pictures was in the hospital bed across from him, from someplace back east; they hung out from that day, went to the Ginza strip, found a sign that said "Heidelberg" — a German restaurant downstairs — and ate there.
researchNotes: Larry has now named the hospital unprompted (2026-08-13 comment): told only that research had a high-confidence candidate — not which one — he wrote "Camp Zama ... in Sugami Uro" [Sagami-Ōno], converging exactly with the documentary case below. The hospital was almost certainly the U.S. Army Medical Center, Japan at Sagami-Ōno / Camp Zama — in Sept–Nov 1965 effectively the only Army hospital in Japan receiving Vietnam evacuees (the 249th General at Camp Drake and the 106th General at Kishine both opened December 1965, after he was home), and documented as admitting 462 Vietnam malaria patients in Aug–Dec 1965; APO 96343 is Camp Zama's. Full research note: research/places/japan-hospital-1965.md. Sagami-Ōno is ~40 minutes from Tokyo on the Odakyū line, an easy day trip to the Ginza for a convalescent. Remaining goals: confirm via NPRC clinical records (filed by hospital name — see research/records-request/); locate the original Stars and Stripes item and ask whether he saw it in the hospital ward; identify the German restaurant of the Ginza day (working leads and next archives in research/places/ginza-heidelberg.md); identify the hospital friend (a fellow patient from back east). Captain "Guegler" may be associated with this period. Coordinates wait on Larry confirming the hospital.
